openers.title: The Magnet Test
openers.question: Two iron(II) salts sit on a balance beside a strong magnet: blue-green [Fe(H₂O)₆]SO₄ is pulled toward the magnet; pale yellow K₄[Fe(CN)₆] is not. Both contain Fe²⁺ with six d electrons. Why does the ligand decide whether the salt is attracted to a magnet?
openers.model_answer: Fe²⁺, d⁶, octahedral. H₂O is weak-field: Δoct < P, high spin, t₂g⁴e_g², 4 unpaired: paramagnetic. CN⁻ is strong-field: Δoct > P, low spin, t₂g⁶, 0 unpaired: diamagnetic. The ligand sets Δoct; Δ against the pairing energy decides the arrangement. (OpenStax 19.3.)
openers.target: In an octahedral field the d orbitals split by Δoct; a strong-field ligand (Δ > P) gives a low-spin complex, a weak-field ligand (Δ < P) a high-spin one.

openers.title: The Pigment Shelf
openers.question: A chemistry stockroom keeps a shelf of coloured coordination salts. A magnetic balance sorts them: some are pulled toward the magnet, some are not. For any octahedral complex on the shelf, how do you predict its number of unpaired electrons?
openers.model_answer: Find the metal's oxidation state and d count; place the ligand in the spectrochemical series; for d⁴–d⁷ choose high or low spin (Δ vs P); fill t₂g and e_g; count unpaired electrons. Example: K₃[CoF₆], Co³⁺ d⁶, F⁻ weak field, high spin, t₂g⁴e_g², 4 unpaired. (Method of OpenStax Example 19.7.)
openers.target: Unpaired electrons follow from the d count, the ligand's place in the spectrochemical series, and Δ versus P.

media.credit: AI image made by the instructor with Gemini

openers.title: The Chromium Rainbow
openers.question: A row of chromium(III) solutions runs from green through violet to yellow as the ligands change, and a spectrometer records each one's absorption peak. Titanium's [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ peaks at 499 nm and looks purple. How does the wavelength absorbed reveal the size of Δoct, and why does the colour change with the ligand?
openers.model_answer: Δoct = hc/λmax: Ti, 499 nm gives 3.98 × 10⁻¹⁹ J/ion = 240 kJ/mol; it absorbs green-yellow, so it looks purple (OpenStax Example 19.9). For Cr³⁺ the absorption moves from the red end into the violet: F⁻ 664 nm (absorbs red; looks green), H₂O 575 nm (absorbs yellow; looks violet), NH₃ 464 nm and en 457 nm (absorb blue; look yellow-orange and yellow), CN⁻ 376 nm (absorbs at the violet edge; pale yellow). Δ rises in the order of the spectrochemical series, and the eye sees the complement of what is absorbed.
openers.target: Δoct = hc/λmax; stronger-field ligands absorb shorter wavelengths, and the solution shows the complementary colour.

media.credit: AI image made by the instructor with Gemini

openers.title: The Humidity Card
openers.question: A humidity indicator card turns blue when dry and pink when damp: blue tetrahedral [CoCl₄]²⁻ gives way to pink octahedral [Co(H₂O)₆]²⁺ as water takes over. Tetrahedral complexes are always high-spin; square planar d⁸ complexes are always paired. Why does the geometry, not just the ligand, decide the electron arrangement?
openers.model_answer: Tetrahedral: four ligands between the axes split the d orbitals into e (lower) and t₂ (upper) with Δtet ≈ 4/9 Δoct, always less than P, so always high spin: [CoCl₄]²⁻, Co²⁺ d⁷, 3 unpaired. Square planar: the d(x²−y²) orbital is pushed far above the rest; d⁸ ions such as [Ni(CN)₄]²⁻ and [PtCl₄]²⁻ pair all eight electrons: diamagnetic. (OpenStax Example 19.8.)
openers.target: The geometry sets the splitting pattern: tetrahedral complexes are high-spin; square planar d⁸ complexes are diamagnetic.

account_given.switch_ask: Where are the ligands, which d orbitals point at them, and what does that do to those orbitals' energy?
account_given.notebook_prompt: I am learning crystal field theory. Explain why the d orbitals split in an octahedral complex, and how Δ and the pairing energy decide where electrons go. Use a complex other than mine. Do not solve any problem for me. Then ask me one short question and wait for my answer.
account_given.return_ask: In your own words, why do some complexes have unpaired electrons and others not?
account_given.park_text: The ligands' electrons repel the metal's d electrons. Orbitals pointing at the ligands rise in energy, splitting the d set by Δ. Electrons then either pair in the lower set or spread into the upper set, whichever costs less energy: Δ against the pairing energy P.

account_given.switch_ask: Both complexes have six d electrons. Which ligand splits the d orbitals more, and what does a large splitting make the electrons do?
account_given.park_text: Cyanide splits the d orbitals so widely that pairing in the lower set costs less than climbing to the upper set: all six electrons pair. Water's small splitting lets them spread out, leaving four unpaired, so that salt is drawn to the magnet.
account_given.show: Here is how a chemist would put it: the six ligands repel the d electrons; the two e_g orbitals that point at them rise by Δoct. Water gives a small Δ, so the six electrons spread out (high spin, 4 unpaired); cyanide gives a large Δ, so they pair in t₂g (low spin, 0 unpaired). Now say it in your own words.

meaning_given.ask: How can the same metal ion form one complex that is attracted to a magnet and another that is not?
meaning_given.switch_ask: What does the ligand change: the metal, or Δ?
meaning_given.show: The metal and its six electrons are the same; the ligand changes Δ, and Δ against P decides whether the electrons pair. Now answer in your own words.
